en: Points of Controversy:
The Chapter on the Path of Certainty,
Ninth Section.
Regarding the discourse on seeing the benefits:
Is there the abandoning of the fetters for one who sees the benefits? Yes.
Is it not the case that the fetters are abandoned by one who attends to mental formations as impermanent? Yes.
If the fetters are indeed abandoned by one who attends to mental formations as impermanent, then surely you should not say:
“The abandoning of the fetters by one who sees the benefits [of practice].
Is it not so that one [views] formations as suffering … as a disease …?
As a tumor...
as a dart...
as a calamity...
as an affliction … as alien … as subject to dissolution …
From pestilence... from calamity...
from fear...
From the perspective of its prefix, from the perspective of its instability, and from the perspective of its perishability...
...of what is impermanent ...
of what is without refuge ... of what is without shelter ...
As being without refuge,
as having become without refuge,
as empty...
as empty ...
as void ...
as non-self ...
Is it not the case that when one attends to [the body] as having danger …pe… as subject to change, the fetters are abandoned?
Yes, they are.
If the fetters are abandoned by one who attends to conditioned phenomena as subject to change,
then surely it should not be said that "the abandonment of the fetters belongs to one who sees the benefit [in them].
And does one attend to conditioned phenomena as impermanent while seeing the benefit in Nibbāna?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Does one attend to mental formations as impermanent and yet perceive the benefits in Nibbāna? Yes.
Is there a convergence of two contacts … pe … of two consciousnesses?
One should not say so … pe …
Does he attend to mental formations as suffering …pe… as subject to change, and yet perceive the benefits in Nibbāna?
One should not say so …pe…
Does he attend to mental formations as subject to change and perceive the benefits in Nibbāna?
Yes. [The same applies to] two types of contact... [and so on].
"Is there a conjunction of two consciousnesses?
One should not say so... [and so forth].
It should not be said—
“Is it not the case that for one who sees the benefits, there is the abandoning of the fetters?”—
“Yes.”—
“Has it not been said by the Blessed One:”

“Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating happiness in nibbāna, perceiving happiness, experiencing happiness, constantly, continuously, and uninterruptedly resolving with his mind and fathoming it with wisdom.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
"Therefore, for one who sees the benefit, there is the abandoning of the fetters.
The Discussion on Seeing the Benefit is finished.
